    AI Overview
    The Jones Act (
    Merchant Marine Act of 1920) is a federal law requiring that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on ships that are U.S.-built, U.S.-owned, and crewed by U.S. citizens. Designed to protect the American maritime industry and ensure national security, it limits foreign competition in domestic shipping. 
    Key Aspects of the Jones Act: 
    • Maritime Restrictions: Foreign-flagged vessels are prohibited from transporting cargo or passengers directly between two U.S. ports.
    • Worker Protection: Beyond shipping, it grants injured seamen the right to seek damages from employers through jury trials.
    • Economic Impact:
      While supporting U.S. shipbuilding and jobs, it is often criticized for increasing shipping costs, particularly to non-continental areas like Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico.
    • Waivers: The law can be temporarily waived for reasons of national defense by the Department of Homeland Security or the Department of Defense. 
    The law was heavily implemented to ensure a strong merchant marine fleet for use during wars or national emergencies.
